[NVIDIA] Lower rounded float conversions with llvm.fptrunc.round (#12237)

Use `llvm.fptrunc.round` for NVIDIA `tt.fp_to_fp` narrowing between f16,
bf16, f32, and f64. This exposes rounding to LLVM and lets NVPTX fold
f16/bf16 conversions through an f32 intermediate into direct SM90+
instructions. It also covers scalar FP16 intermediates in the existing
FP8 conversion paths.

Includes the forward fix in #12407, which should merge first. The LLVM
pin update in #12236 has merged.

- Keep `arith::TruncFOp` on ordinary `llvm.fptrunc`.
- Accept `triton::RoundingMode` in `convertFpTrunc` and stringify it
internally.
- Preserve specialized packed FP8 conversions and migrate
conversion-instruction checks to `tritongpu_to_ptx.mlir`.
- Cover RTNE/RTZ narrowing, f16/bf16 conversions, and FP8 intermediates
in PTX tests for SM80, SM90, and SM100.

Validation on Brix GB300 at `c851915382` with the published LLVM
`18f9e623` build 2 SDK (archive checksum and configured SDK path
verified; LibLZMA discovery disabled):
- Native rebuild and full lit suite: 305 passed, 2 unsupported.
- Conversion suite: 83 passed, 12 skipped, including 10
rounding-boundary cases and exhaustive f16↔bf16 inputs in both
directions.
- Cast/multiply-high tests: 196 passed, 2 skipped.
- FP4 packing regression: 1 passed.
- Pre-commit checks passed.

SM80/SM90 coverage above is compilation through PTX; GPU execution was
on GB300.

Triton CI: all 11 checks passed at `c851915382`
([run](https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/actions/runs/38991161111)),
including A100/H100/GB200, the AMD GPU matrix, gfx1250 emulation, and
macOS.

+    info = torch.finfo(dst_ty)
+    # Values on and adjacent to rounding boundaries, including subnormals,
+    # signed zero, overflow, infinities, and NaNs.
+    positive = torch.tensor([
+        0.0, info.tiny * info.eps / 2, info.tiny * info.eps,
+        info.tiny * (1 - info.eps / 2), info.tiny,
+        1.0, 1 + info.eps / 2, 1 + 3 * info.eps / 2,
+        info.max, info.max * (1 + info.eps / 4), info.max * 2,
+        float("inf"), float("nan"),
+    ], dtype=src_ty)
+    values = torch.cat((positive, -positive))
+    values = torch.cat((values, torch.nextafter(values, torch.zeros_like(values)),
+                        torch.nextafter(values, torch.full_like(values, float("inf")))))
+    values = values.repeat((128 + values.numel() - 1) // values.numel())[:128]
+    # Scale by powers of two and round the significand directly. In particular,
+    # do not use a torch f64 -> bf16 cast, which may round through f32 first.
+    mantissa_bits = {"float16": 10, "bfloat16": 7, "float32": 23}[dst_dtype]
+    min_exponent = -14 if dst_dtype == "float16" else -126
+    max_exponent = 15 if dst_dtype == "float16" else 127
+    reference = []
+    for value in values.tolist():
+        magnitude = abs(value)
+        if not math.isfinite(value) or value == 0:
+            reference.append(value)
+            continue
+        exponent = max(math.frexp(magnitude)[1] - 1, min_exponent)
+        if exponent > max_exponent:

+            reference.append(math.copysign(result, value))
+            continue

+        result = math.ldexp(significand, exponent - mantissa_bits)
+        if result > info.max:

[AMD] Drop core LLVM workarounds after the LLVM bump (#12410)

Triton's core LLVM now includes llvm/llvm-project@5bf967cb132b and knows
the gfx1250-strict processor, so remove the workarounds that bridged the
gap to the independently pinned AMD code generator:

- Remove upgradeLegacyNamedBarriers from the codegen library. Core LLVM
already emits named barriers in address space 15, so restore the plain
parse path, which auto-upgrades debug info. Bump the AMD codegen build
number so the library is republished.
- Derive the amdgpu12.50s triple for gfx1250-strict from core LLVM. Drop
the hard-coded triple, the base-arch layout triple used around core LLVM
target machines, and the TRITON_DUMP_MIR/TRITON_SWAP_MIR restriction for
gfx1250-strict.

Add gfx1250-strict coverage for the target triple, the architected-SGPR
check, and the MIR round trip.

[LLVM] Update LLVM to 18f9e623 (#12236)

Update the consumed LLVM SDK to
[`18f9e623e4c8`](https://github.com/llvm/llvm-project/commit/18f9e623e4c891ba31ff817c07197707ac9bc593),
build 2, which includes the NVPTX `llvm.fptrunc.round` implementation.
All eight checksums come from the successful [post-merge SDK
build](https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/actions/runs/38491954898)
triggered by #12262; all eight published archives are available. Build 2
disables the optional LibLZMA dependency so Linux consumers configure
without liblzma development files.

The LLVM/MLIR update requires these compatibility changes:

- Select NVPTX's `shortptr` ABI and preserve `enable_fp_fusion` through
contraction flags.
- Pass the new `pzo` operand as `false` to NVVM FP32-to-FP16/BF16 and
packed FP4 conversion intrinsics, preserving signed zero.
- Use the typed `LLVM::UMulHOp`, the updated pass APIs, and the new
inline-assembly convergence argument.
- Place AMD named barriers in their dedicated address space, 15, and
update their compile-only tests.
- Parse and restore LLVM TableGen library options alongside `cl::opt`,
so MIR dump/reload honors codegen start/stop points and scheduler
settings.
- Serialize alias-scope domains in the format supported by the
independently pinned AMD code generator, preserving explicit
alias/noalias relationships. Drop only the newer implicit disjoint-scope
guarantee at that handoff.
- Preserve Triton's existing assembly syntax through MLIR's
legacy-properties setting and keep supported attribute-dictionary
builder deprecations as warnings.
- Refresh affected lit expectations for LLVM/MLIR assembly and PTX
printing.

Rebased onto `2122e24efc`. Preserve upstream's `disable_lsr` option
alongside the new LLVM ABI handling. Update the rebased barrier-printing
expectations and remove the obsolete `llc -fp-contract=off` argument.

[ConSan] Synchronize allocation poisoning across CTAs (#11908)

ConSan's poison writes can race with a peer CTA's first access to an
allocation. In particular, a two-CTA MMA can access the peer's TMEM
before that CTA finishes poisoning it, corrupting the result with NaNs.

- Conservatively synchronize all CTAs after allocation poisoning
whenever `numCTAs > 1`, covering both TMEM initialization and
shared-memory initialization. Retain the CTA barrier for single-CTA
kernels.
- Remove the explicit cluster-barrier workaround from
`test_local_indexed_cross_cta_visibility` in
`python/test/gluon/test_consan.py`.
- Move the shared-memory async-proxy fence into `initializeAllocation`.
Emit it after the barrier, using `shared::cluster` coverage for
multi-CTA kernels and `shared::cta` for single-CTA kernels. This orders
the acquired poison stores, including peers' stores, before subsequent
async accesses. TMEM initialization continues to use its store wait.

Add lit coverage for two- and four-CTA TMEM initialization, multibuffer
allocations, single-CTA and disabled-initialization behavior, and
shared-memory initialization on NVIDIA and AMD. Check the proxy fence's
coverage and placement for single-CTA TMA, multicast TMA, and CLC.

Validation: compiler rebuild and both ConSan lit files passed; targeted
GPU tests passed with 99 passed and 20 skipped; `pre-commit run
--from-ref origin/main --to-ref HEAD` passed.

[FRONTEND] Preserve per-result hints through inlining (#12388)

Fixes #12366, Closes #12377

Compiler hints attached to a multi-result `tt.call` currently belong to
the shared operation, so inlining can propagate a hint to the wrong
returned value.

Add a single-result `tt.annotate` identity op and emit it only when
attaching a hint to a value from a multi-result operation. Fold
annotations into single-result producers, retain them for block
arguments and multi-result producers, propagate axis information through
them, and erase them during LLVM lowering. Single-result call hints are
also preserved when inlining returns an argument or a result of a
multi-result op.

Extend the existing inliner lit test for reordered, nested, duplicate,
mixed-rank, and split results. No runtime tests are added. This
addresses the issue described in #12377 while preserving the hints.

[NVIDIA] Preserve unpacked vector loads with a conservative TTI (#12337)

LLVM's generic TTI charges for `extractelement` even when an element
already occupies a separate register. This can make VectorCombine
scalarize an aligned vector load whose elements are all used, obscuring
the vector structure needed by later optimizations.

Add a Triton NVPTX TTI derived from `TargetTransformInfoImplCRTPBase`,
the same generic foundation used by `NoTTIImpl`. Its first override
makes constant, in-range extracts from fixed vectors with 32- or 64-bit
elements free. Sub-word elements, dynamic indices, and other cost
queries retain the generic behavior. This provides a place to add
individually validated target information without adopting the full
NVPTX target-machine cost model.

The NVIDIA backend enables this analysis. Other backends and pipelines
with an explicit target machine keep their existing TTI. The binding
retains an opt-out for differential testing.

Two small synthetic loops illustrate the codegen effect. Each iteration
loads an aligned vector and adds each element to a separate loop-carried
FP32 accumulator. For example, the two-element loop starts with:

```llvm
%v = load <2 x float>, ptr addrspace(1) %p, align 8
%x0 = extractelement <2 x float> %v, i32 0
%x1 = extractelement <2 x float> %v, i32 1
%next0 = fadd float %sum0, %x0
%next1 = fadd float %sum1, %x1
```

With generic TTI, VectorCombine splits the load and the arithmetic stays
scalar. Preserving the vector load lets the existing NVPTX vectorizer
form packed accumulators. Compiling identical inputs with only
`enable_nvptx_tti` toggled (`O3`, SLP disabled, NVPTX vectorizer
enabled, `sm_100a`, PTX 9.4, ptxas 13.4.59) gives:

| Synthetic loop | Generic TTI: SASS per iteration | Custom TTI: SASS
per iteration | Registers, before → after |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Two FP32 accumulators | 2 × `FADD` | 1 × `FADD2` | 8 → 8 |
| Four FP32 accumulators | 4 × `FADD` | 2 × `FADD2` | 14 → 14 |

For the two-element case, the PTX arithmetic changes from two
`add.rn.f32` instructions to one `add.rn.f32x2`. The actual SASS
arithmetic is:

```sass
// Before
FADD R5, R2, R5;
FADD R0, R3, R0;

// After: each operand denotes a pair of FP32 registers
FADD2 R2, R2.F32x2.HI_LO, R4.F32x2.HI_LO;
```

Both versions ultimately use one `LDG.E.64` (two elements) or one
`LDG.E.128` (four elements); the improvement here is packed arithmetic.
The same results hold when loading integer vectors and bitcasting them
to FP32. These are code-generation checks, not runtime speedup
measurements.

<summary>Standalone two-accumulator reproducer</summary>

Save this as `example.mlir`. This is a compiler-only example; its loop
executes at least once.

[AMD] Always insert a workgroup barrier before cluster barrier (#12342)

Currently the compiler does not follow this recommendation as suggested
in the CDNA5 guide 5.6.6:

> It is recommended that waves in a workgroup first synchronize by using
the workgroup barrier, then one wave per workgroup signals the cluster
barrier.

This will cause some troubles, in this minimal case:

```python
# assume a kernel with 2 cta, 8 warp
gl.amd.cdna5.cluster.arrive() # signal  1
gl.amd.cdna5.cluster.wait()   # barrier 1
gl.amd.cdna5.cluster.arrive() # signal  2
gl.amd.cdna5.cluster.wait()   # barrier 2
```

When 2 warp-0 from 2 ctas reached **signal 2** but a slower warp-n has
not yet reached **barrier 1** (n != 0), the warp-n will pass **barrier
1**, but hang at **barrier 2**. As stated in the guide, cluster barrier
is implemented using "Cluster Barrier Wave State", which has a single
bit to indicate that the cluster barrier has completed. So when the
warp-n reaches **barrier 1**, its cluster-completion bit will be
consumed and there is no other wave-0 to set it again given they have
already passed **signal 2**.

The hang can happen in different variants:
1) When the kernel manually uses more than one cluster barrier
2) When the kernel uses more than one consecutive atomics, which under
the hood will insert cluster barriers

A kernel-side remedy is to always insert a barrier before cluster
barrier / atomics. This PR proposes to directly insert it when lowering
the cluster barrier.
